summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans and gender-nonconforming visitors. Nothing in national law protects them, and any visible gender-nonconforming or same-sex conduct in public exposes them to arrest on public-morals grounds.

Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not explicitly criminalised in the penal code. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and same-sex conduct in public draws harsher penalties than other offences covered by the same moral-offence provisions. Reported effects of this regime include a community pushed underground, and social framing of sexual-orientation and gender-identity issues as taboo, imported from Europe and contrary to African values.

The United States State Department's 2023 human rights report states that there are no legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons, that legal gender recognition is not permitted, and that LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military. A visitor whose documents do not match their presentation should expect no legal remedy for the mismatch.

The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman and same-sex marriage is banned. A visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition of that relationship, and affection between same-sex partners in public can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.

There were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights in the country as of the 2023 reporting period, which limits the practical support a visitor in difficulty could reach.
tangentialFactors:
The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights summarised stakeholder submissions for the country's Universal Periodic Review at the forty-fifth session in January 2024; those submissions included recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity. Two earlier Universal Periodic Review recommendations addressed non-discrimination on those grounds and improvements in the situation of sexual minorities.

ILGA World's 2023 survey of laws criminalising LGBT people covers the Central African Republic, and independent legal overviews reach the same conclusion on the penal code: no explicit criminalisation of private consensual same-sex relations, but a public-morals offence that captures public same-sex conduct.

Broader country conditions recorded in United States State Department reporting include extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and armed groups, and harsh prison conditions. For a trans visitor, arrest on morals grounds places them inside that detention environment, where gender-nonconforming detainees face elevated exposure to violence.
localsOnly:
The restrictions described apply to residents as well as visitors. Citizens cannot obtain legal gender recognition, and LGBTQI+ citizens cannot serve openly in the military.

No national legal provisions prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no statutory basis for complaints in employment, housing, health care or public services.

The absence of known LGBTQI+ human-rights organisations means residents lack domestic advocacy, legal-aid and shelter infrastructure, and much of the community's social life remains unorganised and private.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not give the specific penalties attached to Article 85, and no enforcement data on arrests under that provision is available here; the practical frequency of enforcement is unresolved.

Whether the two Universal Periodic Review recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity were accepted or implemented is not sourced in this inventory, and the content of the January 2024 stakeholder recommendations is summarised only at a general level.

The United States State Department's 2012 human rights report for the country contains little LGBT-specific material, so whether the legal position has changed since 2012 cannot be established from these sources beyond the current-state statements above.
